definition: Acerbic means sharp, biting, and bitter in tone.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word acerbic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know acerbic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The museum's audio guide, recorded decades ago by its acerbic founding director, still dismisses an entire gallery as 'furniture with ambitions.'
A tart reply nips and moves on — quicker and lighter than acerbic, which lingers, sour and deliberate, and means to leave a mark.
Venomous goes further than acerbic: the wit drains away and only the poison is left, words meant purely to wound.

Biting words wound with plain force — the insult lands hard and undisguised, and any bully can manage it. Acerbic adds two things biting alone does not promise: a sour flavor and a clever mind behind the sting. A biting remark hurts; an acerbic one hurts and gets quoted.

A barbed remark hides its hook inside something pleasant-sounding — a compliment you only feel sting once you walk away. Acerbic needs no disguise: its sourness and wit sit right on the surface. Barbed is about concealment of the sting; acerbic is about its sour, intelligent flavor.

Acerbic means sharp, biting, and bitter in tone.
Nobody's quilt squares escaped Doris, the sewing circle's acerbic matriarch: 'Lovely colors,' she told one newcomer, 'and if you ever sew a straight seam, they'll be wasted on it.'
Acerbic is more precise than 'mean' or 'harsh' because it names a particular flavor of sharpness — sour, biting, and intelligent.
An acerbic remark stings like citrus in a cut, but there is wit behind it, not mere cruelty.
Reach for acerbic when sharpness comes with brains and a sour twist — a critic's verdict, an aunt's toast.
Its unit-mate vitriolic is the word for when the wit is gone and only cruelty remains; and sardonic, from this unit's own word list, mocks darkly without acerbic's sour sting.

For thirty years the town paper's advice column was written by 'Aunt Vera,' whose replies rarely ran past three sentences.
Her tone was acerbic from the first line to the last: sour, precise, and so quotable that readers saved the column for the answers rather than the questions.
To a man asking how to tell his neighbor that her garden gnomes were tacky, she wrote, 'You don't.
You plant taller hedges and shorter opinions.' New readers sometimes mistook the vinegar for cruelty, but longtime ones knew the wit was the point — the sting made the sense stick.
When she retired, the paper tried three cheerful replacements in a single year; kindness, it turned out, was easier to find than an edge worth quoting.
